title: Initial ridge-spur settlement working landscape
scope: Qualitative local-crown placement, unequal-shoulder managed apron, near-settlement land-cover sequence, lake-road relationship, and layered spring, well, and cistern water arrangement for Project Hearthway's initial ridge-spur settlement. Exact maps, measurements, settlement history and society, detailed infrastructure, hydrogeology, ecology, reliability, and events remain open.
approval_evidence: On 2026-08-15 the Author replied, 'sounds good, i think we go with option A - unequal shoulder apron. As for water supply i think we do a combination of a spring inside the hill-fort/hill-settlement with wells in addition and cisterns for water storage'.
question: What bounded local landscape and water arrangement should give physical form to Project Hearthway's already-established fortified ridge-spur settlement without pre-empting its exact map, society, detailed infrastructure, ecological use, or operational reliability?
selection: Use A — Unequal-shoulder apron. The fortified core occupies the local crown of the already-established ridge spur. An unequal-shoulder managed apron surrounds it: a deliberately maintained low-vegetation warning belt lies nearest the fortified perimeter; beyond it, small and incomplete contour terraces occupy some usable steeper upper slopes; and broader fields and grazing ground occupy the gentler lower shoulder. Woodland resumes beyond the managed apron and comes closer on steep or difficult sides. A constructed road descends in bends toward a lake beyond the immediate apron but within regular local travel and haulage reach. A spring emerges within the fortified perimeter and is incorporated into settlement water access, supplemented by wells and cistern storage. The water elements provide layered access and storage, not guaranteed independent, perennial, potable, inexhaustible, secure, or sufficient supplies.
alternatives: A — Unequal-shoulder apron: fortified local crown with an asymmetric managed apron; selected.
B — Terminal-spur crown: fort at the end of a spur, steep on three sides and connected by one defended neck; not selected.
C — Double-knoll/saddle: higher fortified knoll paired with a lower saddle or second shoulder; not selected.
rationale: The selected option gives the settlement a coherent daily landscape while preserving the accepted separation between its fortified ridge-spur core and WLD-ECOLOGY-004's principal lower-basin crown-herd corridor. Terrain asymmetry supports a compact warning belt, partial upper-slope terraces, broader lower-shoulder working land, nearby difficult woodland edges, and a qualitative lakeward descent without fixing a survey map. The Author's direct combined water instruction adds plausible layers of access and storage while leaving shared hydrogeology, capacity, quality, maintenance, and failure unresolved.
evidence: Author instruction on 2026-08-15: 'sounds good, i think we go with option A - unequal shoulder apron. As for water supply i think we do a combination of a spring inside the hill-fort/hill-settlement with wells in addition and cisterns for water storage'.
consequences: The fortified core occupies the local crown of the ridge spur already established by WLD-ECOLOGY-004; no exact elevation, contour, area, orientation, or relationship to any named place is selected.
An unequal-shoulder managed apron surrounds the crown and extends farther across the gentler lower shoulder, while woodland comes closer on steep or difficult sides.

A deliberately maintained low-vegetation warning belt lies nearest the fortified perimeter and remains distinct from the terraces, fields, grazing ground, and woodland beyond it; the entire managed apron is not established as uniformly bare, short, treeless, or permanently clear.
Small and incomplete contour terraces occupy some usable steeper upper slopes, while broader fields and grazing ground occupy the gentler lower shoulder.

A constructed road descends in bends toward a lake beyond the immediate managed apron but within regular local travel and haulage reach; its exact alignment, turn count, gradient, construction, drainage, destination, distance, travel time, capacity, and seasonal usability remain open.
A spring emerges within the fortified perimeter and is incorporated into settlement water access, supplemented by wells and cistern storage.
The spring and wells may share groundwater, recharge, drawdown, contamination, and drought exposure; no source is guaranteed independent.
Cisterns store finite collected water rather than producing or replenishing water; their source, number, placement, capacity, condition, treatment, allocation, and operational reserve remain open.
No spring, well, or cistern is guaranteed secure, perennial, potable, inexhaustible, adequate, uncontaminated, freeze-proof, drought-proof, siege-proof, magical, or operational.

Exact hydrogeology, yield, recharge, drawdown, connection, water quality, contamination, freeze-thaw response, drought response, treatment, lifting, drainage, sanitation, waste placement, maintenance, and failure remain open.

WLD-ECOLOGY-004 continues to establish exposure around some outer fields, roads, and lake approaches, but this decision does not identify any particular selected field, terrace, or road segment as a secondary-path overlap or guarantee an encounter.
WLD-ECOLOGY-005 continues to govern basin-wide habitat exchange, but no local species, reserve-web presence, food-web use, productivity, or migration is established.
Clearing, cultivation, grazing, road upkeep, water access, and storage use finite land, water, material, energy, and labour and produce persistent environmental and maintenance consequences.

No exact dimensions, population, settlement age, founder, dynasty, council, culture, crop, domesticate, tenure, labour institution, wall design, local rainforest, particular organism, plot event, Mana property, ancient-doorway relationship, offworld influence, or System mechanic is selected.
The selected location has no established relationship to WLD-GEOGRAPHY-002's outlet mixed-reach sequence.
